key_insight: Under declining electricity prices and weak surplus remuneration, shared photovoltaic self-consumption stays viable mainly through collective coordination and adaptive energy-sharing rules rather than through more complex technology alone.
engineering_relevance: For community PV systems, designing governance, allocation, and sizing strategies can matter more economically than adding storage, especially when market incentives for exported solar power are low.
method: Analyzed high-resolution consumption data from a rural PV-sharing community with 24 users.
Compared static, dynamic, and hybrid energy-sharing models, both with and without battery storage.
Evaluated efficiency, fairness, governance complexity, investment cost, and annual savings under current market conditions.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports that collective self-consumption lowers required PV capacity and investment costs while increasing annual savings versus individual operation, whereas battery storage adds limited value except in specific price and remuneration conditions.
watch_item: Results depend strongly on local tariff structures, surplus compensation rules, and the governance capacity of the user group, which may limit transferability.
paper_title: Decision-support strategies for photovoltaic self-consumption under declining electricity prices and limited remuneration of surplus generation
